PAPER: JHSMR Original Article Journal of Health Science and Medical Research Impact of Smear Layer Removal Protocols on Color Dynamics and Dentin Hardness Following Intracoronal Bleaching Kwunklao Saichuea, D.D.S., M.Sc.1, Boonrat Sattapan, D.D.S., M.D.Sc.2, Boonlert Kukiattrakoon, D.D.S., M.S.2, Kewalin Thammasitboon, D.D.S., D.M.Sc.2,3 1Dental Department, Roi-Et Hospital, Roi-Et 45000, Thailand. 2Department of Conservative Dentistry, Faculty of Dentistry, Prince of Songkla University, Hat Yai, Songkhla 90112, Thailand. 3Research Center of Excellence for Oral Health, Faculty of Dentistry, Prince of Songkla University, Hat Yai, Songkhla 90112, Thailand. Received 28 November 2024 l Revised 12 February 2025 l Accepted 18 February 2025 l Published online 10 June 2025 Abstract: Objective: This study evaluated the impact of smear layer removal protocols on intracoronal bleaching outcomes, focusing on color shifts and dentin hardness. Material and Methods: Artificially stained human premolars underwent dentin surface treatments: distilled water, 17% EDTA, and 37% phosphoric acid (PA) before intracoronal bleaching with sodium perborate. Control teeth received no treatment. Tooth color and dentin hardness were measured at 7, 14, and 21 days post-bleaching with a VITA Easyshade spectrophotometer and Vickers hardness tests, respectively. Statistical analysis included Shapiro-Wilk and Levene’s tests, and two-way repeated ANOVA with Tukey’s HSD for shade and microhardness comparison (α=0.05). Results: All the bleaching treatments effectively lightened teeth, with the most pronounced color change (ΔE00) observed after the first week. This was followed by a significant decrease in intensity during the second and third weeks. Color metrics showed reduced redness (a* values) and increased yellowness (b* values) across all the groups, with no significant differences in color change or dentin hardness between the treatments (p-value>0.05). However, a notable decrease in dentin hardness was observed in the cervical sections compared to the coronal sections in all the groups (p-value<0.05). Conclusion: Smear layer removal with 37% PA or 17% EDTA did not significantly improve bleaching efficacy or affect dentin hardness. These findings support streamlined treatment protocols that omit smear layer removal without compromising clinical outcomes. JSON: Name: smear_layer_bleach_effects Title: In vitro spectrophotometric and microhardness assessment of intracoronal bleaching with sodium perborate following smear layer removal using 17% EDTA or 37% phosphoric acid Short Hypothesis: Removal of the smear layer with 37% phosphoric acid or 17% EDTA prior to intracoronal bleaching with sodium perborate mixed with water increases tooth color change (ΔE00) and reduces dentin microhardness compared to no smear layer removal. Related Work: Prior studies have evaluated intracoronal bleaching efficacy and dentin effects across different bleaching agents and smear layer protocols. Work comparing hydrogen peroxide-based protocols vs sodium perborate reports greater dentin alteration and acidity-associated mineral loss with hydrogen peroxide, while sodium perborate mixed with water is less acidic and appears to produce smaller changes in inorganic composition and microhardness. Investigations of smear layer removal using phosphoric acid or EDTA show inconsistent effects: some studies report that phosphoric acid improves agent penetration and enhances bleaching, whereas others report no measurable benefit in shade change or dentin hardness relative to untreated smear layers. Reported limitations across studies include heterogeneous bleaching formulations and concentrations, short follow-up durations (commonly ≤14 days), reliance on visual shade guides rather than calibrated spectrophotometry, limited spatial sampling of dentin hardness, small sample sizes, and lack of standard artificial-staining protocols. These inconsistencies leave unresolved whether smear layer removal yields clinically meaningful improvements in bleaching efficacy or meaningful changes in dentin mechanical properties when sodium perborate mixed with water is used. Abstract: Objective: To determine whether removal of the smear layer with 17% EDTA or 37% phosphoric acid modifies color change kinetics and dentin microhardness during intracoronal bleaching with sodium perborate mixed with water. Methods: An in vitro, randomized, controlled design will compare no-treatment control, distilled-water irrigation, 17% EDTA (60 s), and 37% phosphoric acid (15 s) applied to artificially blood-stained human teeth prior to intracoronal application of sodium perborate/water. Outcomes are spectrophotometric color change (CIEDE2000 ΔE00, L*, a*, b*) at 0, 7, 14, 21 days and Vickers microhardness of inner/outer dentin at cervical and coronal levels. Secondary analyses include SEM verification of smear layer removal and effect-size estimation. Expected contribution: a standardized, adequately powered in vitro pipeline that quantifies whether smear-layer removal alters bleaching performance or compromises dentin hardness for sodium perborate/water bleaching. Impact: results will clarify the necessity of smear layer removal in intracoronal bleaching protocols and inform evidence-based clinical workflow decisions. Experiments: Specimen selection and preparation: Acquire n=120 extracted human single-rooted anterior teeth or premolars (age 18–35 donors) free of caries/restorations/cracks; store in 0.1% thymol until use. Power calculation: detect d=0.8 for ΔE00 with α=0.05, power=0.8 → minimum 24 teeth per group; include 30 per group to allow exclusions. Artificial staining: stain all teeth using standardized human hemolysate protocol (centrifugation cycles and 9–12 days exposure) to produce baseline discoloration; measure baseline shade and assign to groups to equalize mean L* and ΔE00 variance. Randomization: four groups (n=30 each): (1) control (no smear removal), (2) distilled-water irrigation (10 mL/60 s), (3) 17% EDTA irrigation (5 mL/60 s then 10 mL water), (4) 37% phosphoric acid etch (15 s then 10 mL water). Optional positive control subgroup (n=10) with sodium perborate + 30% H2O2. Smear layer creation: prepare standardized access cavities and create smear layer using #4 round bur; standardize buccal wall thickness 2.5–3.0 mm. Bleaching protocol: place sodium perborate mixed with distilled water (2 g :1 mL) into pulp chamber to 3 mm under CEJ; seal with cotton and temporary restoration; replace bleaching paste at days 7 and 14; incubate specimens at 37°C, 100% humidity. Measurements: color: VITA Easyshade Advance or equivalent; three repeated readings per timepoint at 0, 7, 14, 21 days; report L*, a*, b* and compute CIEDE2000 ΔE00. Microhardness: select random 10 specimens per group at each terminal timepoint, embed and section to obtain 2-mm-thick cervical and coronal slices; polish and perform Vickers hardness testing with 50 g load for 10 s at 8 positions (inner dentin 0.5 mm from pulp; outer dentin 1.0 mm from pulp). SEM/EDS: reserve 2 additional teeth per group for SEM imaging at 2,000x–10,000x to verify smear layer removal and examine tubule openness; perform EDS for elemental changes on a subset. Baselines and comparisons: baseline (pre-bleach) measurements for all metrics; primary contrasts: (A) combined smear removal groups vs control, (B) EDTA vs phosphoric acid, (C) perborate/water vs perborate+H2O2 if included. Ablation: within-group timewise analysis removing smear removal step vs with step; additional ablation study: vary phosphoric acid exposure (15 s vs 30 s) in a small subgroup (n=8) to assess exposure dependency. Statistical analysis: test normality (Shapiro–Wilk) and homogeneity (Levene); two-way repeated-measures ANOVA with factors treatment × time for color metrics; three-way mixed ANOVA for microhardness (treatment × section level × distance from pulp); post-hoc Tukey HSD; report p-values, 95% CI, and effect sizes (partial η2). Define clinical thresholds: ΔE00 perceptibility 0.8 and acceptability 1.8. Significance α=0.05. Data recording: blinded operator for measurements; ICC for repeated spectroscopy readings reported. Risk Factors and Limitations: In vitro model limitations: absence of saliva, pellicle, thermal cycling, occlusal forces, and pulpal pressure may alter bleaching agent diffusion and dentin response relative to clinical conditions. Tooth selection and variability: premolar or anterior selection, donor age, prior mineralization and dentin thickness variability may bias results and limit generalizability. Artificial staining: hemolysate staining may not replicate all clinical discoloration chemistries. Measurement sensitivity: spectrophotometer probe positioning and surface wetness can introduce measurement error; Vickers indentations near each other may interact or sample local heterogeneity. Time horizon: 21-day follow-up may miss delayed or cumulative changes in mineral composition or long-term mechanical degradation. Chemical specificity: EDS provides elemental but not molecular-level information on organic matrix degradation (e.g., collagen crosslinking) so mechanisms of hardness change may remain unresolved. Bleaching formulation variability: results apply to specified sodium perborate/water formulation and may not generalize to other concentrations or commercial products. Sample size and multiple comparisons: risk of type I and II errors if effect sizes are smaller than estimated. Clinical outcome translation: changes in ΔE00 and microhardness do not directly predict clinical outcomes such as sensitivity, bonding performance, or risk of external cervical resorption.
